title: Punjab Farmers March on Delhi for Mahapanchayat Against US Trade Deal, Warning of Agricultural 'Devastation'
excerpt: The Samyukt Kisan Morcha is mobilizing over 100 farmer unions for a July 21 protest, calling the India-US trade framework a surrender to American agricultural multinationals.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Punjab farmers are protesting the India-US trade deal, fearing it threatens local agriculture.
  • The Samyukt Kisan Morcha claims the deal favors American agricultural multinationals.
  • Key staples like rice and wheat are excluded from the trade framework, according to the government.
  • NRIs face mixed impacts: potential business benefits versus threats to family farming livelihoods.
  • The July 21 Mahapanchayat aims to amplify farmer opposition and political pressure.
Farmers Unite Against Trade Deal
›Over 100 farmer unions mobilizing for protest.
›Trade deal seen as a threat to Indian agriculture.
›Farmers recall past protests against controversial laws.
›Potential for pan-India agitation if demands are unmet.
  • Punjab farmer unions are mobilizing a Mahapanchayat in Delhi on July 21 to intensify opposition to the India-US trade deal, which they say threatens Indian agriculture by opening the door to subsidized American farm imports.
  • The Samyukt Kisan Morcha (SKM), a coalition of over 100 farm groups, has called the trade framework "a complete surrender" to American agricultural multinationals.
  • The Indian government maintains that sensitive staples like rice, wheat, corn, and dairy are excluded, while basmati rice, spices, and tea growers stand to gain from duty-free US market access.
  • For NRIs, the trade deal carries dual implications — potential tariff benefits for US-India business but also concern for family livelihoods back home in farming regions.

Farmer unions from Punjab are heading to Delhi for a planned Mahapanchayat on July 21 to escalate protests against the India-US trade deal, which farm groups say would devastate Indian agriculture by allowing heavily subsidized American produce to flood domestic markets.

The mobilization marks the latest flashpoint in a dispute that has revived memories of the 2020-21 farm law protests, when sustained farmer agitation forced the government to repeal three controversial agricultural laws.

What Farmers Are Saying

The Samyukt Kisan Morcha (SKM), an umbrella body of more than 100 farmer organizations, has led the opposition. The coalition has called the India-US trade framework "an abject rejection" of government assurances that agriculture would be protected, according to Reuters.

"We are worried about the India-U.S. trade deal, as it would hurt Indian farmers, who are far more vulnerable than their American counterparts."

A Political Flashpoint

Opposition parties have seized on the trade deal as a political weapon."

Farmer leaders argue that American farmers operate with larger landholdings, receive higher subsidies, and benefit from advanced processing infrastructure — advantages that would allow cheap US imports to undercut Indian producers. SKM national secretary Purushottam Sharma warned that lower tariffs on crude soybean oil, currently taxed at around 16.5%, would particularly hurt domestic oilseed producers.

Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Singh Mann has been among the most vocal critics. Speaking in the Punjab Vidhan Sabha, Mann cautioned that the deal "could inflict damage on Indian agriculture far greater than the three black farm laws" and compared the agreement to a modern-day East India Company.

The Government's Defence

Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has repeatedly defended the agreement, saying key staples are excluded from the trade framework. Rice, wheat, corn, dairy, poultry, meat, and several vegetables and fruits — including potatoes, oranges, and strawberries — are not part of the deal, according to Goyal.

Government's Defense of the Trade Deal
›Key staples like rice, wheat, and dairy excluded.
›Basmati rice and spices may gain duty-free US access.
›Minister Goyal argues for potential benefits to exporters.
›Opposition claims lack of consultation with state governments.

The government has pointed to potential benefits for Indian agricultural exporters, arguing that growers of basmati rice, fruits, spices, coffee, and tea would gain duty-free access to the massive US market. Both sides are still working to finalize the written terms of the agreement.

A Political Flashpoint

Opposition parties have seized on the trade deal as a political weapon. The Punjab Vidhan Sabha unanimously passed a condemnation resolution against the proposed deal, with Mann accusing the central government of acting under pressure from the White House.

"No state government has been consulted or even informed about the India-US agreement so far," Mann said in the assembly. "One begins to wonder whether India's decisions are now being influenced by the White House."

The SKM has also pushed back against Goyal's claims, accusing the commerce minister of "consciously propagating falsehood" and demanding his resignation.

Why NRIs Should Pay Attention

For the Indian diaspora, particularly those with family ties to farming regions in Punjab, Haryana, and other agricultural states, the trade deal carries competing implications. On one hand, NRI-owned businesses and professionals involved in US-India trade could benefit from reduced tariffs and expanded market access. On the other, many NRIs maintain deep connections to farming families back home whose livelihoods could be affected if cheap American imports depress domestic crop prices.

The protest also intersects with the broader US-India economic relationship at a time when both countries are navigating trade tensions alongside growing strategic partnership. The outcome could shape agricultural policy for years and affect rural incomes in states that are major sources of Indian emigration.

Implications for NRIs
›NRI businesses could benefit from reduced tariffs.
›Concerns for family livelihoods in farming regions.
›Trade deal intersects with US-India economic relations.
›Outcome may shape agricultural policy for years.

What to Watch

The July 21 Mahapanchayat in Delhi will test the strength of the farmer opposition. If turnout is large, it could increase political pressure on the Modi government to renegotiate agricultural provisions before finalizing the deal. Farm unions have also warned of escalating protests, including a potential pan-India agitation, if their demands are not met.
